preamble: Clues are of two types. In each of the acrosses, the cryptic part leads to the answer to be entered and the definition part leads to an anagram of that answer. In each of the downs, the definition part leads to the answer to be entered and the (cryptic) remainder leads to an anagram of that answer. All grid entries and anagrams thereof (except the anagram of 26 Down) are in The Chambers Dictionary (2008). Bracketed numbers after clues refer throughout to grid entries. Anagrams of entries at 1 Across, 1 Down and 26 Down each consist of two words, that at 26 Down being a familiar phrase not given specifically in Chambers.

clue.text: Old French measure map entering wrong place to fill up at (13, two words)

indicators.note: entering means going inside, so the measure and the map together sit within the word for wrong

parts.note: a tort is a civil wrong in law
the toise was an old French unit of length, about two metres
a plan is a map or drawing of an area

explanation.surface: A muddled motorist pulls in at the wrong spot to refuel, map in hand and thinking in old French units.
explanation.walkthrough: Across rule: the wordplay builds the entry, a succulent also called elephant's foot, while 'place to fill up at' defines PETROL STATION, an anagram of it.
explanation.definitionFit: A petrol station is where motorists refuel their cars, so it is a place to fill up the tank.

clue.text: Parasitic worm: I'll reach tremblingly inside can

indicators.note: inside sets the shaken letters within the can word; under this puzzle's rule that combined word is then rearranged into the entry
trembling letters are shaken about, so the letters of I'll reach are jumbled

parts.note: a can is a tin

explanation.surface: A horror-story warning about a parasite that turns up shaking inside a tin of food.
explanation.walkthrough: Per the preamble, the wordplay of a down gives an anagram of the entry: I'LL REACH jumbled (CHILL RAE) with TIN inside makes CHILL RATINE (a cold rough fabric), and its letters rearranged give the entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Trichinella is the genus of nematode that causes trichinosis, infesting pork and other muscle tissue.

clue.text: Move rapidly, concerned with delay

parts.note: to dart is to move suddenly and fast
re means concerning or about, as in business letters

explanation.surface: Hurry up, given the hold-up.
explanation.walkthrough: Down rule: the definition gives the entry, while the wordplay builds DARTER, one who darts, whose letters are rearranged to give the entry.
explanation.definitionFit: To retard is to slow down or hold back progress, so it means to delay.

clue.text: All-weather track material? Raced round dry one

indicators.note: round wraps the raced word about the dry and one pieces; under this puzzle's rule that combined word is then rearranged into the entry

parts.note: raced means ran
TT stands for teetotal, i.e. dry
A is the article meaning one

explanation.surface: A question about running surfaces, then a runner who sped round a parched track.
explanation.walkthrough: Per the preamble, the cryptic part builds RATTAN (a climbing palm used for cane), an anagram of the entry rather than the entry itself; TT for teetotal is a common crossword convention.
explanation.definitionFit: Tartan is a trade name for a synthetic surface used on running tracks, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Funeral ceremonies gripped with love

definitions.note: the clue's plural stands for the singular entry, a funeral rite or memorial service

parts.note: bit, as in bit down on, means gripped with the teeth
love is zero in tennis, and zero looks like O

explanation.surface: Mourners at the funeral rites held on to one another lovingly.
explanation.walkthrough: Down rule: the definition gives the entry, while the wordplay builds BITO, a small desert tree of Africa and Asia, whose letters are rearranged to give the entry.
explanation.definitionFit: An obit, besides a death notice, is an old word for a funeral service or memorial rite for the dead.

clue.text: Unit for measuring timber forest, top to bottom?

indicators.note: in a down entry the top is the first letter, here sent to the foot of the word

parts.note: a forest is a mass of trees

explanation.surface: Timber is measured in the forest from treetop to root.
explanation.walkthrough: Down rule: the definition gives the entry, while the wordplay builds REEST, a Scots word meaning to balk or refuse to move, whose letters are rearranged to give the entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A stere is a cubic metre, the metric unit used to measure stacked firewood and timber.

clue.text: Piebalds drink up measure of water displaced

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the drink word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: to sip is to drink in small mouthfuls
a displacement ton measures a ship by the weight of water it displaces

explanation.surface: Patchy horses drink up at a trough, spilling a measure of water.
explanation.walkthrough: Down rule: the definition gives the entry, while the wordplay builds PISTON, whose letters are rearranged to give the entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Pintos are horses with patchy white and dark markings, which is what piebald horses are.

clue.text: Plant juice essential for muscular lesions

parts.note: essential for points to letters held inside the next words: they run across the end of muscular and the start of lesions

explanation.surface: A plant extract said to be essential for healing torn muscles.
explanation.walkthrough: Down rule: the definition gives the entry, while the wordplay builds ARLES, Scots for earnest money, whose letters are rearranged to give the entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Laser is an old name for the gum resin of silphium and related plants, valued in antiquity.

clue.text: Blue stuff marked track for swimmers, we hear

indicators.note: we hear signals that the result only sounds like the swimmers' track

parts.note: a lane is a roped-off strip of a pool for one swimmer

explanation.surface: Blue dye has marked the swimmers' lanes, by the sound of it.
explanation.walkthrough: Down rule: the definition gives the entry, while the wordplay builds LAIN, which sounds like lane, whose letters are rearranged to give the entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Anil is the indigo plant and the deep blue dye made from it.

clue.text: Slit in the sea: how it all began (11, two words)

indicators.note: in sets the slit word within the sea phrase; under this puzzle's rule that combined word is then rearranged into the entry

parts.note: rit is a Scots word meaning to slit or scratch
the sea is the ocean, with the article kept

explanation.surface: A biblical-sounding image of the sea splitting open at the dawn of the world.
explanation.walkthrough: Per the preamble, the remainder gives an anagram of the entry: RIT inside THE OCEAN makes THEOCRITEAN (in the pastoral style of Theocritus), whose letters rearranged give the entry.
explanation.definitionFit: The Creation is the biblical account of God making the world, the beginning of everything.

clue.text: Listen to piece in your headphones

indicators.note: a piece in the following words is a run of letters lying inside them, across the word break

parts.note: the bird's name runs across the end of your and the start of headphones

explanation.surface: Listen to a track playing in your headphones.
explanation.walkthrough: Across rule: the wordplay builds the entry, a South American flightless bird, while 'Listen to' defines HEAR, an anagram of it.
explanation.definitionFit: To hear something is to listen to it, a plain verb synonym for paying attention to sound.

clue.text: Works trim first sign of overmanning

parts.note: to pare is to trim by cutting away the edge

indicators.note: the first sign of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: only its first letter is used

explanation.surface: A factory cuts staff at the first hint of overmanning.
explanation.walkthrough: Down rule: the definition gives the entry, while the wordplay builds PAREO, a Polynesian wrap skirt, whose letters are rearranged to give the entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Opera is the plural of opus, a composer's numbered work, so it means works.

clue.text: Ethereal maiden, a help when retiring

indicators.note: retiring means drawing back, so the phrase for a help is read from its end to its start

parts.note: an is the form of a used before a vowel, as in an aid
an aid is a help

explanation.surface: A delicate girl is a useful helper whenever she withdraws.
explanation.walkthrough: Across rule: the wordplay builds the entry, the Roman goddess of the hunt, while 'Ethereal maiden' defines NAIAD, an anagram of it.
explanation.definitionFit: A naiad is a water nymph of Greek myth, a spirit maiden of springs and rivers.

clue.text: Clubs hospital accommodating footballing legend

indicators.note: accommodating means the hospital word houses the legend's name; under this puzzle's rule that combined word is then rearranged into the entry

parts.note: san is short for sanatorium, a hospital
Pelé is the Brazilian football legend

explanation.surface: Football clubs and a hospital caring for a great former player.
explanation.walkthrough: Per the preamble, the remainder gives an anagram of the entry: SAN holding PELE makes SPELEAN (relating to caves), whose letters rearranged give the entry. 'Clubs' looks like football teams but means cudgels.
explanation.definitionFit: An alpeen is an Irish cudgel, a heavy stick used as a weapon, so the plural is a set of clubs.

clue.text: Saint, mature man of God

parts.note: ripe means fully developed or mature, as fruit or cheese is

explanation.surface: A saint described as a mature holy man.
explanation.walkthrough: Across rule: the wordplay builds the entry, a band or line of colour, while 'man of God' defines PRIEST, an anagram of it.
explanation.definitionFit: A priest is an ordained minister of religion, a clergyman serving God.

clue.text: Flowering plant is briefly seen in East African river

indicators.note: seen in places the shortened word inside the river's name

parts.note: the Nile flows north through East Africa to the Mediterranean
is shortened to its contracted form 's leaves just the letter S

explanation.surface: A flowering plant spotted growing along an East African river.
explanation.walkthrough: Across rule: the wordplay builds the entry, to store fodder in a silo, while 'Flowering plant' defines SILENE, an anagram of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Silene is the catchfly or campion genus, a group of flowering plants of the pink family.

clue.text: Keep scratching last in Civil Service

indicators.note: in places the word for last inside the letters for the Civil Service

parts.note: latter means the last of two, as in the former and the latter

explanation.surface: A civil servant who can't stop scratching until the very end.
explanation.walkthrough: Across rule: the wordplay builds the entry, makes rattling noises, while 'Keep scratching' defines SCRATTLE, an anagram of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Scrattle is a dialect verb in Chambers meaning to scratch or scrabble about continually.

clue.text: Thin plates mum put in a row

indicators.note: put in sets the mother word inside the row phrase; under this puzzle's rule that combined word is then rearranged into the entry

parts.note: ma is a familiar word for mother, like mum
a row is a line, with the article kept

explanation.surface: Mother lining up thin plates in a neat row on the dresser.
explanation.walkthrough: Per the preamble, the remainder gives an anagram of the entry: MA put into A LINE, and those letters rearranged give the entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Laminae is the plural of lamina, a thin layer, scale or flat sheet of material.

clue.text: Injury involves active bitterness

indicators.note: involves means takes in, so the injury word holds the letter for active

parts.note: harm is injury or damage

explanation.surface: An injury that leaves the active victim feeling bitter.
explanation.walkthrough: Across rule: the wordplay builds the entry, Arabic for forbidden under Islamic law, while 'bitterness' defines MARAH, an anagram of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Marah is a Hebrew word for bitterness, from the bitter waters the Israelites found in Exodus.

clue.text: With e.g. Brighton ahead, monarch briefly turned back

indicators.note: ahead puts the seaside town's description in front of the monarch's letters

parts.note: Brighton is a seaside resort on the south coast of England
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the short form of the Queen's title

explanation.surface: With Brighton in sight, the Queen ordered the royal coach to turn round.
explanation.walkthrough: Across rule: the wordplay builds the entry, someone who frequents a place, while 'turned back' defines RETRORSE, an anagram of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Retrorse is a botanical term for something pointing backwards, like hairs bent towards the base of a stem.

clue.text: Herb, one planted in places of research

indicators.note: planted in means set inside, so the numeral goes into the research rooms

parts.note: labs, short for laboratories, are where scientists do research

explanation.surface: A herb grown in research laboratories.
explanation.walkthrough: Across rule: the wordplay builds the entry, the spoon used for communion in the Eastern Church, while 'Herb' defines BASIL, an anagram of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Basil is an aromatic culinary herb of the mint family, used widely in Italian cooking.

clue.text: We'll fill niche, looking up, than which one can sink no further

definitions.text: than which one can sink no further

indicators.note: fill means the pronoun occupies the inside of the reversed niche word; under this puzzle's rule that combined word is then rearranged into the entry
in a down clue looking up means the word reads from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: a niche is a slot
read as we will, giving the pronoun we that does the filling

explanation.surface: A promise to fill a gap that is looking up, set against reaching rock bottom.
explanation.walkthrough: Per the preamble, the remainder builds TOWELS, an anagram of the entry rather than the entry itself; 'looking up' signals the upward reading because this is a down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Something at its lowest is at the bottom point, beneath which no further descent is possible.

clue.text: My old rose, initially without thorns

parts.note: mine is the old form of my, used before a vowel, as in mine eyes

indicators.note: initially takes the opening letter of the next word

parts.note: only its first letter is used

explanation.surface: My old rose bush, which at first had no thorns.
explanation.walkthrough: Down rule: the definition gives the entry, while the wordplay builds MINER, whose letters are rearranged to give the entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Inerm is a botanical term for unarmed, having no spines or prickles.

clue.text: Shaping again what local goes to at Doncaster?

parts.words: what local goes to at Doncaster?
parts.note: a Yorkshireman goes to t'races, the races, at Doncaster racecourse

explanation.surface: Remodelling where the locals go at Doncaster, home of the St Leger horse race.
explanation.walkthrough: Down rule: the definition gives the entry, while the wordplay builds TRACES, whose letters are rearranged to give the entry. Yorkshire speech clips the to t'.
explanation.definitionFit: To recast is to remould metal or rework something into a new form, so it means shaping again.

clue.text: A maiden always: special bowler

parts.note: taken as written
M is the cricket scorebook abbreviation for a maiden over
e'er is the poetic contraction of ever

explanation.surface: A cricket bowler who always delivers maiden overs, a special talent.
explanation.walkthrough: Down rule: the definition gives the entry, while the wordplay builds AMEERS, Muslim rulers, whose letters are rearranged to give the entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A seamer is a cricket bowler who makes the ball deviate off its seam.

clue.text: Pressing tasks? Abo woman knocked back turps extract

indicators.note: knocked back, like a drink downed, means the woman's word is read backwards

parts.note: gin is an old Australian word, now offensive, for an Aboriginal woman
rosin is the resin left when turpentine is distilled from pine gum

explanation.surface: Urgent chores await while an Aboriginal woman downs a drink of turpentine.
explanation.walkthrough: Across rule: the wordplay builds the entry, a black dye, while 'Pressing tasks?' defines IRONINGS, an anagram of it. The question mark flags pressing as clothes, not urgency.
explanation.definitionFit: Ironings are the loads of laundry to be smoothed with an iron, the chores of pressing clothes.

clue.text: Wiseacre taking King in is furious

indicators.note: taking, paired with the later in, means the wise-person word absorbs the king's letter
in completes taking ... in; under this puzzle's rule the combined word is then rearranged into the entry

parts.note: a wiseacre, ironically, is a sage
R is the abbreviation for rex, king

explanation.surface: A know-all who lets the king in is livid about it.
explanation.walkthrough: Per the preamble, the remainder gives an anagram of the entry: SAGE taking R in makes SARGE (a sergeant), whose letters rearranged give the entry.
explanation.definitionFit: To rage is to be violently angry, so one who rages is in a fury.

clue.text: Conceited person despatching jay: perfect score

indicators.note: despatching means getting rid of, so the bird's name is removed

parts.note: a popinjay is a vain, strutting person, from an old word for parrot
the bird's name, taken as written and removed from the end

explanation.surface: A vain man disposes of a jay with one perfect shot.
explanation.walkthrough: Down rule: the definition gives the entry, while the wordplay builds POP IN, a familiar phrase for a brief visit, whose letters are rearranged to give the entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Ippon is the full point in judo, a decisive throw or hold that wins the contest outright.

clue.text: Mole blood vessel injected with Ecstasy

indicators.note: injected with means having something put inside, so the drug's letter goes into the vessel

parts.note: vena is the Latin and anatomical name for a vein

explanation.surface: A spy shoots ecstasy into a vein.
explanation.walkthrough: Across rule: the wordplay builds the entry, the Indian stringed instrument, while 'Mole' defines NAEVE, an anagram of it. Mole looks like a spy; here it is a skin blemish.
explanation.definitionFit: Naeve is an old form of naevus, a birthmark or pigmented spot on the skin such as a mole.

clue.text: Cereal crop, good with light breeze

parts.note: an air is a light, gentle breeze

explanation.surface: A cereal crop does well with a gentle breeze.
explanation.walkthrough: Down rule: the definition gives the entry, while the wordplay builds GAIR, whose letters are rearranged to give the entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Ragi is finger millet, a grain grown as a staple food in India and Africa.

clue.text: Top bit of masonry to choose round most of cover

indicators.note: round means surrounding, so the choosing verb wraps the shortened cover word

parts.note: to opt is to choose

indicators.note: most of drops the last letter of the cover word

parts.note: to encase is to cover completely

explanation.surface: A builder must choose how to cover the top stone of a wall.
explanation.walkthrough: Across rule: the wordplay builds the entry, mining done from the surface, while 'Top bit of masonry' defines CAPSTONE, an anagram of it.
explanation.definitionFit: A capstone is the finishing stone that crowns a wall or structure, its topmost piece of masonry.

clue.text: One's highly strung, quite energized in part

parts.note: in part points to a piece of the preceding words: the letters run across the end of quite and the start of energized

explanation.surface: A nervy teenager is quite wired, at least partly.
explanation.walkthrough: Down rule: the definition gives the entry, while the wordplay builds TEEN, whose letters are rearranged to give the entry. Highly strung suggests nerves; it means the top string.
explanation.definitionFit: Nete was the highest string of the ancient Greek lyre, the one sounding the top note.

clue.text: Sour porter maybe: one brought in light beer

indicators.note: brought in means put inside, so the letter for one goes into the beer

parts.note: lager is a light, pale beer

explanation.surface: One sour porter is brought in for a light beer at the bar.
explanation.walkthrough: Across rule: the wordplay builds the entry, a camp ringed by wagons, while 'Sour porter maybe' defines ALEGAR, an anagram of it. Porter here is the dark beer, not a doorman.
explanation.definitionFit: Alegar is ale that has gone sour, malt vinegar, so soured porter is an example.

clue.text: Cartographer, American, absorbed by homework?

indicators.note: absorbed by means taken inside, so the American letters sit within the homework word

parts.note: prep is British school slang for homework, short for preparation

explanation.surface: An American mapmaker engrossed in homework.
explanation.walkthrough: Across rule: the wordplay builds the entry, an amplifier stage before the main one, while 'Cartographer' defines MAPPER, an anagram of it.
explanation.definitionFit: A mapper is someone who draws maps, the plain word for a cartographer.

clue.text: Old-fashioned adventure tale, say, is in French

parts.note: e.g., for example, means the same as say
est is French for is

explanation.surface: A quaint adventure story, for instance, told in French.
explanation.walkthrough: Across rule: the wordplay builds the entry, to discharge waste from the body, while 'Old-fashioned adventure tale' defines GESTE, an anagram of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Geste is an archaic word for a tale of heroic exploits, a medieval romance of adventure.

clue.text: I'll come after section leaves

indicators.note: come after places the self after the letter for section

parts.note: read as I will: the ego is the self, the I

explanation.surface: Someone promises to follow once a section has gone.
explanation.walkthrough: Across rule: the wordplay builds the entry, a North American lily, while 'leaves' defines GOES, an anagram of it. Leaves looks like foliage; it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Goes is a plain synonym for leaves, as in departs from a place.

clue.text: Cockney bum suffering torment, against protesting strongly? (13, two words)

parts.note: aris is Cockney rhyming slang for backside, via Aristotle, bottle, bottle and glass, arse

indicators.note: suffering shows these letters in distress, so they are scrambled into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
on can mean against, as in leaning on a wall

explanation.surface: A Londoner with a sore backside protests loudly against the agony.
explanation.walkthrough: Across rule: the wordplay builds the entry, Greek for 'moderation is best', while 'protesting strongly?' defines REMONSTRATION, an anagram of it. The question mark marks a noun defined by a verb phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Remonstration is a forceful protest or objection, the act of remonstrating.
